subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The Senate have made to Bill No. 70, to amend the Weights and Measures Act, several amendments, all of which except one it is desired to concur in. The first amendment is to section 1 of the bill, adding to the statute a new paragraph (f) defining the expression "pre-packaged goods." The proposed amendment is to add the following as subsection 2 of section 1:
(2) Section two of the said act is further amended by adding the following as subparagraph (f)- _
(f) the expression "prepackaged goods" or "prepackaged articles" includes any article which is packaged or made up in advance ready for resale in a wrapper or container, and where any article packaged or made up in a wrapper or container is found on any premises where such articles are packaged, kept or stored for sale, the article shall be deemed to be packaged or made up in advance ready for retail sale unless the contrary is proved.
There is no difficulty about that.
Weights and Measures Act

The next amendment proposed by the Senate is to section 8 of the bill, page 3, where in line 25 the word "and" is struck out and replaced by a comma in the interests of charity and good English. That amendment may be accepted without question.
The next amendment is to section 10 of the bill, page 4, which amends section 63 of the act which by the bill is repealed and a new section substituted therefor. Section 10 of the bill is the section that sets up new penalties for short weights, measures or counts. In the bill as drafted and passed by this house the minimum penalty for a first offence was a fine not exceeding $50, and the Senate have amended that by reducing the minimum to $10. For a second offence the minimum set up by the bill as passed by this house *was $100 and the Senate amendment reduces that to $50. That is accepted.
The Senate have also amended section 10 by adding thereto a new subsection (4) which provides:
(4)	No proceeding shall be taken under the provisions of this section in respect of prepackaged goods or articles if the person proceeded against has already been convicted under section twenty-three of the Food and Drugs Act, of a breach of the provisions of section seven, paragraph (f) of the said act in respect of the same goods or articles.
The idea is that a person accused should not be convicted under two different acts for the same offence. I think that is perfectly sound.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The minister in reading the amendment said section 17, but the amendment reads section 7.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
It is section 7 of the Food and Drugs Act. Perhaps the right hon. gentleman did not catch my statement. The idea is that if the person against whom the proceedings are taken under the Weights and Measure Act has been already convicted under a similar section of the Food and Drug Act no proceedings shall be taken on the same set of facts. The two acts more or less overlap, and that amendment I think is quite in order.
But the Senate have added a further subsection (5) to section 63 of the Weights and Measures Act with respect to an alleged deficiency of weight or measure of prepackaged goods. I will read the amendment as passed by the Senate:
(5)	In any proceedings under this act in respect of an alleged deficiency of weight or measure of any prepackaged goods, the court shall disregard any inconsiderable variation in the weight or measure of a single article, and
[Mr. R. B. Hanson.1
shall have regard' to the average weight or measure of a reasonable number of other articles of the same kind, if any, sold or delivered by the defendant, or in his possession for the purpose of sale or delivery, on the same occasion.
Very considerable thought has been given to that proposed amendment by the departmental officials. The subsection put into the act by the Senate is substantially similar to a section of the imperial Sale of Foods Act, 1926 (Weights and Measures) 16 and 17 George V, chapter 63, and was placed in the imperial act as "a safeguard to traders." In the imperial act this safeguarding section is unquestionably justified, as that act establishes two offences: (a) sale of prepacked article short weight; (b) having in the trader's possession for sale or delivery, prepacked article short weight. Section 10 of the imperial act gives weights and measures inspectors authority to inspect prepacked articles and to compel the sale of any short weight article disclosed on any such inspection. In view of the offence created by paragraph (b) mentioned above this safeguarding section is quite reasonable.
It is pointed out that the Canadian Weights and Measures Act establishes only one offence, namely, sale by short weight, and the weights and measures inspectors, if short weight in prepacked goods is disclosed upon inspection, have no authority to compel sale to secure evidence of an offence, such as they have in the English act.
In this connection I am advised by the field officers that the trader generally refuses to sell short weight prepacked articles to them for evidence, in which he is quite within his rights in our statutes. It is submitted that this safeguarding section is unnecessary and should be deleted. Should it remain it is pointed out that the enforcement of section 63 as amended by the Senate is going to be seriously handicapped and the courts placed in a quandary in applying this section to any offence taken to prosecution, in which the accused may set up the defence that the articles in question were prepacked and claim the protection of the section.
The offence of sale by short weight under our act is disclosed by test purchases made by the independent shoppers. In a test purchase of four items, should two be short weight an offence is undoubtedly established. If these two short weight items be "prepacked" then this section applies, and the following difficulties will have to be considered: (a) How can the article in hands of an independent shopper be identified as a

Weights and Measures Act
prepacked article (b) How can "reasonable number of other articles of the same kind"- that is the language of the section-be inspected and found short weight "on the same occasion"-those are the words in the English act-when only one was purchased.
I need only point out that difficulty to gentlemen of the legal profession to have them appreciate the point (c) Should the short weight item be brown sugar for instance, would a package of tea short weight for the second item be an "other article of the same kind" under this section? (d) Would short weight in the trader's store, found on an inspection after the test purchase was made, be on "the same occasion"? These difficulties as set out, it is submitted, practically nullify section 63 of the act in so far as it applies to its enforcement against prepacked articles, and it is thought by the officers of the department that we cannot accept the Senate amendment.
Other amendments made by the Senate are such as can readily be accepted. For instance, section 15, page 5 of the bill, has been amended by the Senate by inserting the words "guilty of an offence and." Also the same words have been inserted in section 16 after the words "shall be" in line 7. I may say that I suggested the insertion of these words myself but the draftsman said they did not matter and he overruled me as I did not like to enforce my own opinion against his.
The next amendment is to section 17, page 6 of the bill, where the Senate have struck out the section altogether, and the officers of the department agree that section 80 of the existing act should be repealed. That has to do with the sending of inspectors from one district into another. If the section is repealed the limitation which was on the authority of the inspectors to go from one district into another will be removed entirely. The section as drafted in the bill gave authority for the inspectors to go in, but it is pointed out that if we repeal the section altogether there will be no question about their authority.
Then the Senate have amended section 18, page 6 of the bill, by inserting the word "lawfully" in line 26 of the new section 82A. I would have assumed no regulation would be of any effect unless it was made lawfully, but if it is considered that the word "lawfully" should be used, of course there is no objection.
The Senate have added another section to this bill at the end thereof, section 19.

speechtext:

was. Section 81 (a) was added in committee and the bill was reprinted before it went to the Senate. A new section 19 was added by the Senate, as follows:
The said act is amended by inserting the following section immediately after section eighty-two thereof:
82a. In prosecutions under sections sixty-three and sixty-four of this act-
Those are the short weight and unjust scales sections, the two important sections of the act.
-although absence of mens rea shall not be a defence it may be deemed to affect the amount of penalty to be imposed in the circumstances and as to that issue it may be proved.
It will be recalled that in the Canadian Weights and Measures Act there is no necessity of proving intent to deceive. In the English act they have inserted the principle of mens rea. This is a compromise position, I should say, between the two points of view. The officers of the department take the ground that if you have to prove guilty intent you will never get a conviction. This proposed amendment provides that while it is not necessary to prove guilty intent the absence of mens rea may be taken into consideration by the magistrate in amelioration of the offence. I think perhaps that is quite right, and I think this house will agree to the amendment.
I think I have covered all the amendments, with one possible exception. In section 16, amending section 77 of the act, they have added the words, "guilty of an offence" in the twenty-first line. That is agreeable to the government. In view of that, therefore, I move:
That all the amendments made by the Senate to amend the Weights and Measures Act. be concurred in except subclause (5) of section 10. proposed to be added to the bill by the sixth amendment, which is not agreed to for the following reasons:
If allowed to stand, this section would practically nullify section 63 of the Weights and Measures Act in so far as its enforcement in connection with prepackaged articles is concerned.
Evidence of short weight under the Weights and Measures Act must be obtained by a test purchase, usually made by independent shoppers.
Such being the case, it is pointed out that to get the "average weight or measure of a reasonable number of other articles of the same kind on the same occasion" is clearly impossible. It is not practicable to purchase wha.t might be considered "a reasonable number of articles of the same kind" and an
Weights and Measures Act

inspection of prepackaged articles in a store by an inspector, either before or after the making of a test purchase, is not "on the same
occasion."
The trad'er is adequately safeguarded against picayune or vexatious prosecutions, by the fact that all proceedings under section 63 of the act must receive the consent of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in writing.
The amendment proposed' by the Senate is substantially the same as section 10 of the imperial Sale of Foods Act. In addition that act provides that an inspector can compel the trader to sell him short weight articles as evidence for prosecution when short weight in prepackaged articles is found on inspection on the trader's premises.
Such authority is not contained in the Canadian Weights and Measures Act, which renders the proposed amendment unnecessary while making the enforcement of section 63 extremely difficult in so far as prepackaged articles are concerned.
And I should add:
And that a message be sent to their honours acquainting them with the attitude of this house.

speechtext: I regret that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) has not decided to redeem the tax-free bonds outstanding, even though they mature in 1937. It is most absurd that the government should lose this large amount of income. The suggestion has come from this side of the house in order that the revenue should be increased. The government should follow this suggestion as it would be appreciated throughout the country. I ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) who were holding these bonds but I received no answer. When the by-election was being held two years ago in Restigouehe-Madawaska I told the electors the particulars of the questions I had asked to which I had received no satisfactory answers. The limit of taxation has been reached and as the Prime Minister said, not this year, not the year before but two years ago, it is time that those who have the money should pay. At the present time those who have no money have to pay it all. This country is becoming alarmed because of the advantages given to the privileged few who are exempted from taxation while the common man, the man on the street has to pay for everything. Even members of parliament who have no means at all have had a cut of ten per cent in their indemnity until this year, when it was reduced to five per cent. We must pay this while our responsibilities are so great. The government should be strongly censured in this connection.

This government has issued no tax-free bonds nor have any been issued for many years. If my hon. friend would apply his very astute mind to the problem of finance I can assure him that he will discover that if we were to go into the open market to buy these bonds at the price at which they are now selling we would lose money. That procedure would cost us much more than to redeem them at par value when they mature in 1937. It is a question of dollars and cents and if the government could save money by entering a transaction of that kind it would gladly do so.

speechtext:
That is a very nice answer but it is ambiguous. One must consider the time when these bonds were issued. They were issued during the war to give an opportunity to the profiteers and the sharks to take advantage of the treasury of this country by not having their profits taxed. It must be remembered that it was the Toiy union government which issued these tax-free bonds

Trade and Industry Commission
in order to give a chance to the profiteers to keep their profits without carrying a part of the burden of taxation. This is what was done with loan after loan. The government was not imposing much taxation, it was borrowing money and the next Liberal administration had to look after the payment of the debt of Canada which was out of all proportion.
We hear a lot about the sanctity of contracts but what about the sanctity of the British North America Act which has been destroyed by this government. This government has had no regard at all for the constitution of this country but when it comes to protecting profiteers they invoke the sanctity of contracts. It would seem as though the Minister of Finance was a high priest. This government reminds me of Lytton Strachey who spoke about a crank who thought he was Adam, Melchisedec and the Lord himself. That is what the Prime Minister thinks, that he is Adam, Melchisedec and the Lord himself but it does not impress me at all. I can speak just as loudly as he can. Very often the Prime Minister speaks in a loud tone to prevent people from seeing that his knees are trembling. I can speak just as loudly as he can; I do not suffer from a heart attack and he does not either; I can speak even louder than he can. I want to be heard by all hon. members, I want to be heard by the Prime Minister even though he feigns sleep at the moment. Let me wake him up when I tell the people of this country that he cannot protect the profiteers by being unwilling to redeem these tax-free bonds.

speechtext:
That only strengthens what I was about to say. The essence of the report as I read it, is that the Combines Investigation Act is the important act, and what the commission recommends is that its provisions should be strengthened as much as possible. Had the government extended the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act so as to put its administration under a commission specially qualified and appointed for that purpose, it would then have been carrying out the intent and purpose of the royal commission in the matter. But what the government is doing now, instead of appointing a commission that will be primarily charged with the important function of administering the Combines Investigation Act, as was the price spreads commission's intention, is to place that act under a body already in existence for the purpose of dealing with the tariff, thereby subordinating the Combines Investigation Act and the carrying out of its provisions in a very material way. In other words, the tariff board has already pretty much all the business it can attend to if it is going to attend to it properly. It will be found, I think, if the tariff board is asked what length of .time it will take to complete the work it has already on hand, the reply will be that there is enough on hand at present to keep the board busy for another year. To add to the functions of the board the business of carrying out the provi-



Trade and Industry Commission
sions of the Combines Investigation Act is simply to sidetrack the Combines Investigation Act altogether. The Combines Investigation Act is the important measure, and while there may be the strongest reasons for extending its provisions in a way that would serve to bring into being a special commission in the nature of a trade and industry commission to carry out the provisions of the act more effectively, this particular method of dealing with the matter is, as I have said, simply negativing in large part the benefits that already exist under the act.
Members of the tariff board are, I think admirably qualified for some of the work they are doing at the present time; at least the chairman is; I am not speaking of the other members. But I question very much whether even the chairman has the sympathy with the Combines Investigation Act that will incline [DOT] him to give most of his time and attention to its provisions, rather than to deal with matters affecting the tariff as he has been accustomed to doing since his appointment to that office. The administration of the Combines Investigation Act is of such importance that whoever has charge of the administration of that measure should be particularly concerned with protecting the public interest in the manner in which the act makes evident it was the intention that the public interest should be protected; in other words, that the interests of the community at large should in every particular override where they come into conflict with those of any special interests. I may be wrongly informed, but if I am not mistaken the chairman of the board himself has been acting for some of those interests in the past, not that I believe this would make the slightest difference to his attitude in administration, but it does suggest that in the government's mind there has not been the effort to secure for the administration of the Combines Investigation Act the type of person who the public generally would feel was the one who . should be specially charged with the administering of that measure. What I want to stress is that the tariff board with what it is already doing has just about all it can do if it is going to do that properly. Under this bill it is not merely the administration of the Combines Investigation Act that is being added to the duties of the tariff board; it is going to have to do with the administration of such other matters as price and production agreements, commodity standards, prosecution of unfair trade practices, fair trade conferences, cooperation with boards of trade, investigation into general economic and social fMr. Mackenzie King.]
conditions, and the supervision of security issues. When all of these obligations are added to the board's present obligation, I think the Combines Investigation Act will pretty well fade out of the picture.
But may I point out to the minister that the tariff board has already had the power to hold inquiries similar to those which are being held under the Combines Investigation Act, but in all the years the tariff board has been in existence, nothing of that character has been referred to it or attempted by it. Subsection 4 of section 4 of chapter 55 of the statutes of 1931, establishing the tariff board, reads as follows:
The governor in council may empower the board to make any investigation or hold any inquiry authorized by the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act, or of a relative nature, and for these purposes the board shall have all the powers, authority and jurisdiction vested in the registrar or in a commissioner appointed under that act to hold investigations.
The tariff board has already all these powers and there is no need to confer these powers upon it for the administration of the Combines Investigation Act because the board already has those powers, although it has never exercised any of them. If the government had reason to feel that the Combines Investigation Act was not being administered as effectively as it should be by those in charge of it, it might have taken advantage of this provision, but it never did do so. It can do so in future, under existing legislation, if it so desires. While I sympathize with the government's desire in not wanting to have an undue number of commissioners, it seems to me that they have appointed new commissions where there was no need of any, and here where there would be justification for enlarging the provisions of the Combines Act to place its administration under a commission specially for that purpose, in view of the obligations cast upon it, they are taking the opposite step. I think the government is making a great mistake.

The Prime
Minister has referred to the section which places this act under the president of the privy council. I had intended to refer to that point when we reached that section, but we slipped by the section so quickly that I had not a chance to do so. Personally I think that is a mistake. This session we have heard a good deal about the extent to which the Prime Minister is overtaxed in connection with the duties of his office and the many obligations Which attach to it. During my right hon. friend's absence from the house because of ill health occasioned by overwork we had a long discussion here on the very question as to whether some arrangement might not be made with respect to the Prime Minister's office which would give him more in the way of assistance to carry out the duties of that office. Now this act proposes to place on his shoulders the responsibility for the tariff board which is to have additional obligations with respect to the administration of the Combines Investigation Act and other matters.
I think that is a mistake. I am assuming that whoever holds the office of Prime Minister will also hold the office of president of the privy council, and I do not think it is possible for the Prime Minister, in his capacity as president of the privy council, to give the attention that should be given to the administration of acts of this character. They ought to be under separate ministers of the crown. To-day the Minister of Finance has the responsibility with regard to the tariff board and the Minister of Labour has the responsibility with respect to the Combines Investigation Act. In questioning the Minister of Labour in regard to the Combines Investigation Act we discovered that he was not as familiar with what was being done under that measure as this house had reason to hope and expect he would be. I cannot see how the Prime Minister is going to find it possible to devote to this additional work the time and thought which should be given to it. There again I think that the government by ithis measure is subordinating the importance of the Combines Investigation Act and the significance that should be attached to its work.
I can sympathize with the view of the government in not wanting to appoint more
commissions than are absolutely necessary. I do not know whether or not the government considered giving the officers now charged with the administration of the Combines Investigation Act additional help in the way of some legal assistance. I think if the act had been amended to make provision for a director of prosecutions and possibly a director of publicity, two such officers functioning under the new provisions of the act would have been infinitely more effective in carrying out its intent and its provisions than any staff, no matter how large it may be, which may have to do with the act as transferred for purposes of administration to the tariff board. I feel that here there is a move in the wrong direction. I am glad to gather from what the Prime Minister says that there will be an opportunity to test out the arrangement during the ensuing year, that he sees the need for further consideration of and no finality in the present step. I hope in that interval, while this transfer is taking place, the matter will not be left in such shape thait the whole effect of the Combines Investigation Act will be nullified for the time being, or in any degree for all time. That is one feature to which I shall wish to direct attention a little later on, but I think it should be kept in mind at this time.

speechtext: I had intended to reserve my remarks for section 20, but as the matter has been brought up I may say a few words here. I have. a business difference with someone; we both want to be fair but each thinks the other fellow unfair, and according to our own -lights we are both right. It may be said that the courts will deal with it. But the business of the court is merely to determine whether a definite and specified offence has been committed. It is not the jurisdiction of the court to define the offence, apart from the confines of the act itself. This is an important question; it is given a headline by itself-unfair trade practices. If you say that each court will deal with the matter then we shall have a different version from each court. If the minister will turn to section 2, paragraph (h) he will find that there are enumerated -twenty-five different acts and some thirty sections of the criminal code, which are defined as laws prohibiting unfair trade practices. It may be that some of them do, the Live Stock Act, for instance; but the majority of them do not define in so many words what an unfair trade practice is, and if you have no definition anywhere in the act it becomes an important question as to how the matter is to be dealt with. subtopic: ADMINISTRATIVE, ADVISORY AND INVESTIGATORY FUNCTIONS-PROVISION FOR A DIRECTOR OF PUBLIC PROSECUTIONS
speechtext:
This is a controversial clause. I just want to repeat what I said on the second reading. As a minority member of the price spreads commission I am opposed
to this clause as are the other Liberal members of the commission. It authorizes the formation of agreements regulating price and production; that is to say, it authorizes the sanctioning of combines by the governor in council on the recommendation of this commission. Perhaps the major activity of the dominion trade and industry commission is the prevention of combines, the enforcement of the Combines Investigation Act, and this clause to a very considerable extent may effect the nullification of that act. Clause 14 is a sort of echo of the NRA; it makes this body into a code forming or code sanctioning authority and authorizes what has always been illegal in this country, that is the formation of combines in industries for the purpose of enhancing prices and limiting production, which inevitably is to the prejudice and detriment of the consumers. I went into this question fully in my remarks on the second reading of the bill, and it is not necessary for me to repeat what I said then.
I admit certain safeguards have been inserted in this clause. Apparently those who drafted it realized that they were doing something very drastic when they introduced this principle into legislation; it is not anywhere else on the statute books except in the Natural Products Marketing Act. They drafted it so that the commission must be unanimous, and they also by the last words of the last subclause indicated that under some circumstances prosecutions for violations of the Combines Investigation Act might be possible even though those who had entered into the price and production agreement were merely following out the agreement. The concluding words of the clause are entirely inconsistent with the purpose of the clause itself. But I am not objecting to those concluding words; I am objecting to the whole clause as entirely at variance with the principle of the Combines Investigation Act, and unwise, unnecessary and injurious. The Natural Products Marketing Act was passed to authorize producers of natural products to enter into such agreements. It went further and authorized manufacturers of products made from natural products to enter into such agreements. Therefore you have this absurd situation: two code sanctioning authorities set up within the last two years to authorize combines which are monopolies. The whole tenor and principle of the price spreads report, the whole doctrine that underlies it, is that one of the greatest evils in Canadian contemporary life is monopolies and monopolistic combines. The introduction of this provision in the statute implementing the recommendations of the

Trade and Industry Commission
price spreads report, while it does follow the recommendation of the majority, is something which in my judgment should not be done. I could not say any more than that if I talked for a long time.

speechtext:
I quite
understand the hon. gentleman's point of view, and he has put it forward both on the second reading and again to-day in a very moderate way. But I disagree with him when he suggests that this is not a beneficial thing. I should like to point out to this committee and to this house and the country that this section of the bill is aimed at cut-throat competition. It is an attempt to give effect to agreements which will not be detrimental to the public interest, and then only after the fullest investigation and report.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATIVE, ADVISORY AND INVESTIGATORY FUNCTIONS-PROVISION FOR A DIRECTOR OF PUBLIC PROSECUTIONS
speechtext:
I am
using the word generally-not detrimental to the public interest. The hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. IMery) says there is an inconsistency in the language of the section when you read the first one or two subsections with the last subsection. But I suggest there is no inconsistency, because if the agreements are such that they are not detrimental to the public interest, then they are not in violation either of the Combines Investigation Act or of the criminal code, and no offence has been committed. Subsection (1) reads:
II. (1) In any case where the commission, after full investigation under the Combines Investigation Act, is unanimously of opinion that wasteful or demoralizing competition exists in any specific industry, and that agreements between the person engaged in the industry to modify such competition by controlling and regulating prices or production would not result in injury to or undue restraint of trade or be detrimental to or against the interest of the public, the commission may so advise the governor in council and recommend that certain agreements be approved.
That is one thing-investigation and recommendation. Then subsection 2 provides for approval and review by the governor in council. It says:
The governor in council may, if of opinion that the conclusions of the commission are well founded, approve of any such agreement, and shall make regulations requiring the commission to determine from time to time whether the agreement is resulting in injury to or undue restraint of trade or is detrimental to the public interest.
Then subsection 3 provides for information and rescission of approval, which of course is a safeguard; and subsection 4 provides that

there must be the consent of the commission for prosecution. I should like to put this to the committee. We have had in this country for a number of years now cut-throat competition in newsprint production. Our production of newsprint, apart from the small percentage that goes into domestic consumption, about which I do not think there is very much trouble, is largely for export. It is one of the products which Canada produces in large quantity and exports, bringing new wealth into the country. We all know, if we know anything at all or are interested in and 'have been following the newsprint situation in recent years, the tremendous cutthroat competition there has been in that industry to the detriment of Canada; I think that is a fair statement-to the detriment of this country. If we had had the machinery in the last five years or longer under which we could have had governmental approval of fair trade agreements respecting newsprint for the export trade, I think it would have been to the great benefit of Canada.

speechtext:

I say that if we had had anything like that, then in my humble opinion, and I am putting it forward with great humility, it would have been of great benefit to the newsprint industry, and consequently of benefit to Canada. I can think of other examples. Look at the situation of the furniture industry in Canada to-day-every reserve of every company wiped out. Ask our colleague across the floor what is the position of the furniture industry in Canada today as a result of cut-throat competition. I put this query to the committee: Is it in the public interest that an old established industry in Canada like the furniture industry-I see my hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young) is ready to spring; I may possibly bo stirring up trouble-should be subject to such conditions as have existed in the industry for the last few years. Mr. Chairman, this section
provides that wherever wasteful or demoralizing competition is found to exist in an industry, those engaged in the industry may be permitted to formulate agreements to regulate prices and production, in other words to form some sort of combine. Now, wherever wasteful or demoralizing competition exists in an industry it is generally the result of overexpansion, and overexpansion is generally the indication of a lack of judgment on the part of somebody engaged in the industry. When we find that condition existing should we permit those who have been guilty of this lack of judgment and have overexpanded their industry to come together and form an agreement to regulate production and fix prices? Should we not in that case be doing something that was detrimental to the public interest? We are deliberately keeping more people in an industry than the country can afford to maintain in it, and by that very act we are doing something against the public interest.
The minister mentioned the furniture industry as an example. Let us take that industry. In this country we had a great many furniture factories producing furniture which the people of Canada were buying. Then, with the coming of the depression, the people lost a large percentage of their purchasing power. They simply could not buy as many goods as they had been buying, and furniture was one of the things they could do without, so furniture was one of the things they first stopped buying. If this clause had been in effect at the time and our furniture manufacturers had1 come together to form an agreement to limit production and fix prices, what good would it have done them? The people would not have bought their furniture in any case, and the higher they kept their prices the

Trade and Industry Commission
less furniture the people would have bought. The only way furniture went into consumption at all was by cutting prices. I know of a young man in this very city who got married and wanted to furnish a house. The depression was on and he saw that prices were coming down, but he said, "We cannot buy our furniture yet, but presently prices will come down." So he waited and waited, but apparently some understanding was arrived at among the furniture dealers of this city and this young couple could not buy their furniture until they discovered that someone in Toronto was selling furniture at lower prices. So they went to Toronto and bought their furniture for less money, and in that way they gave employment to people in the furniture industry which they never would have done if there had been an agreement such as this.

I am coming to that.
I realize the soundness of that statement, but all one has to do is take the history of the railways of the United States in the years 1850, say, to 1880. There is a classic work upon that subject. They were unrestrained and unrestricted, and the traffic had to pay what it could bear. I think those were the words of one of the famous creators of railways in the United States. Then there was a great system that gave rebates to one of its largest customers. They were secret rebates, known only to the railway company and the customer. That history is a matter of record. The result was that the people of the United States came to the conclusion, as did the people of England, that there ought to foe a body created that would fix the same rate for the same service for all railways. I am just pointing out what the result was with respect to carriers. They were common carriers competing with one another in the same area for traffic, at any price at which they could get it, ostensibly showing certain rates which in fact they overcame by giving secret rebates. As I say, that history is one of the most interesting that one

Trade and Industry Commission
could read. The United States found it necessary, as did Great Britain and Canada, to set up a board that would fix the same rate for the service rendered, having regard to what is called water competition east and west and the other factor, that is, where you have traffic to be carried to two ports, one of which is a little greater distance' than the other, the rate to the further distant port is the same as it is to the lesser distant port. Without going into details those were the principles.
Now let uls go a step further. Then came what are known in the United States as the great packer cases. In that country it was found that the packers drove out of business the small butcher who bought and killed local cattle and sold them in his own market. He was being driven out by the car that stopped at the siding. Usually before that took place the padker offered the local man the chance to sell out; sometimes he sold and sometimes he did not. The whole matter was reviewed by the Supreme Court of the United States, and the oil cases were also reviewed by that court at great length. The result of unrestricted and unrestrained competition was the creation of monopoly. The very thing my hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young) aims to prevent was brought about by unrestrained and unrestricted competition. In the end the survival of the fittest meant a monopoly, with great resources, with many branches and with activities extending to all parts of the world. Now let us see what we had in this country during the years to which reference has been made. My hon. friend from Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) said it was a case of over expansion. In very buoyant days the prospects of high profits from certain forms of industrial activity so affect others that they go into the business when purchasing power is high and large, and there being no reserves set up to meet the situation because of the effect of continuing competition there is undoubtedly great over production in periods of depression. The real truth is that because our combines act read as it did there came about large numbers of mergers. The mergers were the direct result of unrestrained competition, resulting in one corporation that created a monopoly in many communities and afforded no protection at all to the consumer. They were within the law, because twenty, thirty or forty plants had been carried into one plant, which did not come within the combines act. Therefore they could no longer be investigated as combines. I say to the hon. members for Hants-Kings and Weyburn, does it not come down to a choice between one of two things: Shall we permit the creation of a condition that will prevent the growth of monopolies and the creation of monopolies, by adequate restriction and regulation, or dhall we permit the unrestrained operation of free competition to the destruction, ultimately, of all but the fittest?-and I am using the word "fittest" in the sense of meaning the largest resources. That is the position, as it appears to me-and I regret to say that I have come to this conclusion, because all my life I have followed with some interest this class of transaction. Hon. members who are members of the legal profession, and who will take the trouble to read the judgment of the Supreme Court of the United States will recall that the former ambassador to Great Britain, Mr. Kellogg, acted in several of these actions. There you have an illustration of another phase of the matter. Take tobacco, take oil, take packers, take the steel industry-all these matters were carefully considered and investigated; litigation was launched, in some cases with success and sometimes with failure. In the supreme court reports you will find in very comprehensive detail all the matters to which I have referred.
In this country we make no distinction between export and domestic business, so far as combines are concerned. The hon. member for Hants-Kings has suggested that there might be no opportunity for prosecution-

The public interest of
Canada, yes. But, just to finish what I was going to say: The Sherman Act, so-called in the United States, was an act not unlike our Combines Investigation Act-I say, not unlike it. In general terms the decisions of the Supreme Court of the United States would apply with equal force to the provisions under our combines act.
There is an important distinction between the principles which govern British law and those governing the law of the United States. The great case in English law was the Great Mogul steamship case, where the ship lay in harbour and could not get a cargo. Certain prohibitions were brought about, and the House of Lords decided as there was no statute in the matter it could not be said to be against the public interest to do what was being done, because there was a regulation of trade and

commerce in accordance with what they conceived to be a good and sound principle, and they did not interfere in that case.
About the same time in Brantford, Canada, there was a case in which a decision was arrived at indicating that under the provision of the criminal code there was no liability. A little later I defended what was known as the lumber combine case in the province of Alberta. I can recall the facts vividly, although it must be twenty-five or more years ago. When the papers were submitted to me I was clear that upon eleven counts they could be acquitted, but that upon the twelfth count I saw no chance of acquittal under the statute as it stood, because they were enabled to fix a price, inasmuch as they endeavoured to limit the creation of lumber yards by saying that a new yard should not be opened at a given point, without their permission. If ft was opened without their permission there was no opportunity for the unfortunate man who opened the yard to secure a supply. In my judgment it was quite obvious that that violated the provisions of the secticn. Accordingly the case was tried before Chief Justice Sifton, and he acquitted my client upon eleven counts and found him guilty upon the twelfth count. That is an illustration of what I conceive to be proper conviction, because the regulation undertaken by t'he industry within itself was not such regulation as was in the public interest. In other words, it placed in the hands of the industry itself-I shall put it this way-the power to determine the terms and conditions under which people should be able to buy what is a necessary product in that province, namely lumber.

That is what we are endeavouring to do.
Let us leave out a discussion of the desirability or otherwise of monopoly. None of us wants monopolies; we do not want them in these days. Of course there are monopolies respecting telephones, and various other matters of that kind. That question- has been discussed in a judgment delivered by the House of Lords in which the whole economic situation was reviewed. But, leaving that for the moment, we come to the second problem which -confronts us: How can we create a condition by legislation which

will ensure the benefits of a reasonable price to the consumers and at the same .time prevent the maintenance of monopolies? Yes. I put that to the committee. How otherwise can we do it? One, two, three and four arrive at an agreement. The agreement is that the profits resulting from their efforts shall not exceed either a percentage upon the turnover or a rate upon the business transactions, but shall be according to some agreement that commends itself to the commission as being reasonable. I believe the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Hanbury) was right, namely, that we should not provide for inefficient business. We have always objected to inefficient business being made the standard of measurement with respect to operations, or anything else. There is nothing more injurious than, as was done in one case in Canada, to the detriment of every consumer, to take an inefficient 'business and make it the standard1 for the determination of tariff assistance or aid. You cannot do it. Efficiency is the first factor in determining whether or not there shall be a grant of tariffs to an industry. Speaking about inefficiency, I have in mind a case which was brought to my attention since I have been in office where the complaint was made that they could not make money. The answer was clear: "You cannot make money with obsolete machinery." You cannot make money or you cannot have a return unless you have good management and unless you have proper machinery. The unfortunate position is, as we have it in industry to-day. that you cannot do by man power that which is being done more effectively by machinery by a competing company. For instance in the cotton industry there are great mills. One mill in Canada is possibly equal to any mill in the world. But, what has been the result in Japan? Why is Japan in such a fortunate position to-day? Because Japan has efficient machinery and management, and in some cases is working in competition with old and worn out machinery.
The problem, I repeat, is this:	How can I
save one, two, three and' four by ensuring that they get a relative share of all the business, and at the same time prevent the destruction of one, two and three by number four, which has a monopoly of the whole business and takes one, two and three out of production. I know of no way in which it can be done other than by providing that these people make arrangements among themselves. subtopic: ADMINISTRATIVE, ADVISORY AND INVESTIGATORY FUNCTIONS-PROVISION FOR A DIRECTOR OF PUBLIC PROSECUTIONS
speechtext:
My purpose in rising is not to question what the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was saying earlier in the discussion with respect to unrestrained and unrestricted competition having led to mergers and monopolies but to take issue with what my right hon. friend said as to the combines act having in any way been responsible for the creation of mergers. That statement has been made by hon. gentlemen opposite from time to time, and, I think, wholly without any justification. Mergers have been part of the order of the day during the last quarter century or more and they certainly had become extensive at the time the Combines Investigation Act was first



Trade and Industry Commission
introduced in 1910. The purpose of that act was not to preclude mergers or combines, as it was recognized that, with world competition what it was becoming, large combinations of capital as well as of labour were part of the inevitable trend. In the light of that it was felt desirable that there should be enacted legislation which would prevent those large combinations which were likely to become more numerous and more powerful from operating in a manner which would be detrimental to the public. The offence was not the formation of a combination, a monopoly or a merger; it was the operation of these powerful combinations in a manner which was detrimental to the public interest. This whole question was gone into fully before the price spreads commission and in the light of the frequent representations from some hon. gentlemen opposite, including the former Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), the commission made a very definite statement on the point. In dealing with the administration of the combines act, the commission report on page 266 as follows:
We regard the first, a rigorous enforcement of the combines act, as most important.
And continuing:
The act does not by its terms, or by the manner of its present enforcement, hamper any combination that would operate in the public interest,-
That statement could not be more definite, and that is made, I gather, as the result of the discussion and consideration of that very point. My right hon. friend mentions that the combines act is very similar to the Sherman anti-trust act and that the Sherman anti-trust act had been directed specifically against combinations as such. That is perfectly correct with respect to the purpose of the Sherman act, but at the time our Combines Investigation Act was introduced the difference on the point in question between the Sherman act and our act was made clear to the house when it was considering the measure. It is true that certain provisions of both measures are very similar, for example those that have to do with investigations. The difference is that in the Sherman act a trust qua trust is an offence and is considered a combination detrimental to the public interest whereas under the Canadian Combines Investigation Act it was set forth frankly at the time of its introduction that in the order of things it might be expected that these large combinations would increase and that it was therefore necessary to prevent their exercising their power against the public interest. The offence that was set forth was the antisocial practices of any species of

combination. The. Combines Investigation Act might equally well have been called the mergers investigation act or the trusts investigation act or the monopolies investigation act as all were placed exactly on the same footing in the original act and are exactly on the same footing in the present act.
While I am speaking on this section there is another point I should like to bring up with reference to the report of the price spreads commission. The commission emphasized emphatically the necessity of the need of more effective control of monopolies and especially the enforcement of one or two provisions of the present combines act with respect to the lowering of tariffs or the withdrawal of certain patent rights in the event of offences occurring under the act where a remedy might be afforded through either of these methods of redress. I do not see anything in the legislation which the government has brought forward thus far to indicate that it is taking any action with respect to the recommendations of the commission as to the control of monopolies. This afternoon, when the
Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was speaking, he referred to competition leading to monopoly and I .think his argument was something like this: that where you have free competition the more efficient gradually gobble up, shall I say, the less efficient, and the numbers of those engaged in the industry are gradually reduced until the more efficient have a monopoly of the business. I wonder how many monopolies we have in this country that have grown up and have perpetuated themselves on that basis and that basis alone. Apart from what we might call natural monopolies, such as railways, telephones and so on, have we a single monopoly in this country that has not been fostered and is not living to-day by reason of some special privilege granted to it, aside from the efficiency of the operation of that business? I doubt whether we have a single one. As business grows bigger it becomes harder to manage and ultimately it reaches the point where efficiency is impossible in that business. One of the chief causes of inefficiency is 'bigness; there is a limit to what the human mind can manage. I was talking the other day to a man engaged in the warehousing and trucking business, the manager of a small company, and he told me he was in direct competition with one of the largest concerns in the dominion; and he said, "We can undersell them, we can undercut them everywhere. We can handle at 40 cents a ton a commodity which would cost them 70

cents." I asked him how this was possible and he replied, "Because of the very size of the concern. It costs a tremendous amount of money to be efficient."

Now how will you secure efficiency in an industry which is not exposed to competition such as that? The competition of the smaller concern will force the larger concern to become efficient or go out of business, or will undermine the larger concern in the end. Without that competition, and with such an arrangement as is contemplated in this bill, how will you provide that efficiency for the larger business? It cannot be done. The competition of the other concern is the only thing that will drive them to it. Mr. Carlisle, president of the Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company, came before the price spreads committee and told us that in 1920 a 30 x 3| tire sold for $25.35; to-day that same tire sells for $3.96 and the mileage, he said, had been doubled. You have industries 1, 2, 3, 4, located in communities 1, 2, 3, 4; are you going to allow competition to destroy industry No. 1, industry No. 2 and industry No. 3, and the communities that depend on those industries? If they had told the government at that time that they would not be able to supply us with the same quantity and quality of goods we had been using before at the prices we had been paying before, they would not have got the protection even from my right hon. friend. him that they would not raise the price. Technically they did not, but practically they did by reducing the quality, with the result that the people of this country had to wear fewer clothes than they were wearing before and the wages paid by the industries were reduced. Although imports of textiles from other countries were shut out, the Canadian manufacturers did not supply the deficiency, and I frankly accuse them of breaking faith with the government; for when they come and ask for a market for themselves, they are under a moral obligation to supply that market without any decrease in the supply or in the value.
Under this legislation it will be possible for those people to come together and agree on prices and terms which will make it unnecessary for them to compete with efficient producers in either their own country or abroad. As I said before, as concerns get bigger and bigger, it is harder and harder for them to become efficient. Left as they had been, if there were no competition from abroad, more efficient concerns would develop in this country and force them out of business or to become efficient. But under this legislation, once they reach a certain point they can get together; all they have to do is to cut prices under one another and then they can get permission under this legislation to form a combine and have a gentleman's agreement which will fix prices and make the people pay on the industry's cost of production and not on a basis of efficient production.

I do not want to leave the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) under a misapprehension; if what I said to-day left the impression that I was dealing with Canadian industry, I was not; I was talking about the recapitalization of business that had been sold to the public so many times in Lancashire. It will be recalled that at the very time we were dealing with the problem, there was a reduction by the courts in England in the capital structure of one of the enterprises by a sum that amounted in our money to millions. I am mentioning that only lest there should have been a misapprehension.
All trusts popularly so-called have not been offences against the Sherman act. The steel trust, so-called, won its case in the Supreme Court of the United States; Mr. Kellogg was able to convince the court that it did not contravene the provisions of the Sherman act. In this country what the leader of the opposition has said is true: the question of the public interest has been the test to be applied under the combines act's powers.
In the criminal code we still use the word "undue." I daresay many members have read Mr. Herbert's Misleading Cases in which he refers so humorously to "the reasonable man" that no one has ever been able to discover, who determines the issue in al cases. That is what is meant by the difficulty of determining what is unfair, undue. I purposely did not touch this point this afternoon because it is not a proper thing to compare the scale of wages and things of that sort in other countries with that which obtains in our own. If the hon. member will take the trouble to read the Sunday number of the New York Times of two weeks ago yesterday, he will find a complete report upon the whole situation with respect to the cost of production. One of the very difficulties we are labouring under to-day in connection with our dealings with Japan is the question of cost production.
As regards efficient machinery, I desire to repeat that there is in Canada a cotton mill that has as efficient machinery as there is in the British empire, if it is not more efficient than any other. The second hand machinery thajt my hon. friend referred to and .that came into Canada was efficient machinery, but it was because of the shifting of the business from northern United States to the south where cotton is produced, that the very best machinery that could be manufactured had to be sold and either moved down to where the cotton was grown or else brought into this country. That so-called second hand machinery contains the last word in manufacture in the way of patented methods for 'the production of textiles cheaply, just as the shoe making machinery that was sold by this continent to the countries of Europe has enabled them by improving on it to sell their boots in once free trade England and other parts of the world in successful competition against evpry other producer. I have given some attention to this question for some years, for a period of twenty years ana more as a matter of fact, if that information is of any use to the hon. gentleman, and I will confess that whenever I found a government institution set up for the purpose of giving its imprimatur of approval to the issues of securities, it has created a difficulty because it is then relied upon. Notwithstanding all that you may say to the contrary, that fact remains. As will be observed, this section contemplates new security issues, which the Secretary of State may refer to this board for investigation. All new security issues do not require to be investigated; no one suggests that they do. A moment ago the hon. gentleman spoke of the door being locked after the horse is stolen. I am sure ne was not deliberately exaggerating when ihe made that statement; surely he has not looked at the provisions of the Companies Act, with respect to what I conceive to be the governing factor, namely the prospectus upon wnich securities may be sold. The law as it will be passed by this parliament will meet the difficulty that we have experienced! in times past, of prospectuses being issued wnich have avoided making tne statements that I conceive to be necessary tor tne purpose of informing the public as to the true condition of the companies wnose securities are being sold. I may say that at one time I thought the purpose would be served by endorsing across the face of the share certificate in red ink that the property covered by the security issues of this company cost the promoters so many dollars. The prospectus as outlined in the Companies Act, as it will be amended by the act now before the house, is far stronger than that. It goes further; it meets the difficulty I have always experienced, the difficulty that probably most of us who have practised corporation law in days gone by will clearly appreciate. That is this: When the exploiting promoter got hold of the company he secured all its common shares, its preferred shares and its bonds for so much money, without determining how -much was for bonds, how much for preferred shares and how much for common stock. Then he sold them as the purchaser of them, and the terms of the prospectus of the company, or the statement in lieu of prospectus, left him entirely out of the picture. As a result the

public was 'hooked; that is the short way to put it. Now I do submit that the amendments proposed by the Secretary of State meet that situation.

What the Secretary of State raised was the question whether it might not be an interference with property and civil rights in view of the fact that in the case before the privy council it was held that the security frauds act was intra vires of the provincial legislature in respect of provincial companies. It will foe recalled that the case arose in Alberta and part of the court was of opinion that we could not interfere with a federal company in connection with these matters. The privy council took another view; it held that the province had certain powers that it could properly so exercise. The Secretary of State has nothing to guide him with respect to what the effect of that decision may be upon our powers in that regard, but the Secretary of State has inserted the provision that any purchaser, any broker, who buys these securities now must buy them on the terms of that prospectus which must be in the terms set out in the statute. That is the most advanced legislation we have had so far in this country to protect the public against fraud with respect to these sales of securities. I suppose the hon. gentleman knows from his practice, as well as I know, how difficult it has 'been adequately to safeguard the investing public by any suggestions that may be made. I have seen one suggestion after the other brought forward and tried, and if my own observation may be worth anything it is that the security frauds acts as enacted by the provinces probably have gone as far as any legislation that has been passed in Canada in that regard, but we had to go another step forward. It is the old story of publishing a statement in lieu of a prospectus and then having the securities sold as I have indicated, that enabled the irregularities to be created that brought about the scandals to which reference has been made.
Certainly in the legislation now before the house we have overcome that difficulty as the Secretary of State has said. Without desiring to express an opinion that might be open to question, in view of the security frauds case, as to how far the provinces may go in that matter, my own view is that we have followed the principle of law laid down by the privy council that when you have power to create something you have power to impose the
conditions under which it shall exercise the powers that have been conferred upon it. When we create a corporation we say that one of the conditions under which that corporation may part with its securities is that the purchase of those securities by the promoters or the brokers shall be upon the terms of the prospectus, which shall constitute the terms of the bargain.
I think in fairness my hon. friend will regard that as a very distinct advance; I do, at any rate. The other evening the hon. gentleman indicated that I had no idea of my own intentions in the matter. Well, I am much older than he and I practised my profession for a considerable number of years before coming he.re. I have given a considerable amount of time 'to the study of that problem. Certainly I make no claim to any special knowledge of it, but I do say that in the discussions I have had with the Secretary of State for the purpose of trying to safeguard the public in connection with the sale of these securities, we believe we have gone further than anything that has 'been done before in Canada with that end in view. I do not intend to discuss the Companies Act to-night; that will come later, but I still think the section dealing with watered stock is one of the most difficult of all sections to deal with. I am still opposed to no par value shares, and if the price spreads commission had recommended that they be abolished I would have been glad to support that recommendation, but they were careful to suggest the alternative. They have given the imprimatur of their approval to no par value shares, to which I am opposed personally and against which I shall vote in this house i.f the opportunity arises. I a.m still against them.

But the Companies Act
is an entirely different .measure from these others. That is an act in connection with which recommendations were made, and the price spreads commission were not specific in that sense. I said to the Secretary of State, as he stated to the house the other day, that I believed it was a measure of such a character that every member of the house should be free to express his views and take the course that might- suggest itself to him as the best way to serve the public interest. That is why the Companies Act is in that form. If the opportunity arises, however, I still will vote against no par value shares. There is an article in the last issue of the Canadian Bar Review, written I think by a gentleman in Montreal, which is well worth reading. He also
Trade and Industry Commission

is opposed to no par value shares as I am, but it does not follow that the price spreads commission may not have been right in saying that the alternative view is quite as sound as the view which I hold. Therefore I do not desire to say that I have any monopoly of wisdom with respect to that matter. It may well be that the members of the price spreads commission and those associated with that work were right in recommending the alternative suggestion to the Canadian people rather than the abolition of these shares, but the reasons given in the article to which I have referred I think are such as will commend themselves to anyone. So this country is able to have a revising, reviewing body in the case of new securities without giving the imprimatur of governmental sanction and without the necessity for referring to this body the issues of every new company created. If the law with respect to prospectuses is observed, and if the law with respect to watered stock is observed-and I shall discuss that phase of the matter when the time comes- under this section, namely:
The commission shall in any case, if requested by the Secretary of State, investigate and review the capital structure of any company incorporated by or under any act of the parliament of Canada, proposing to issue new shares, debentures or other securities to the public
-We cannot deal with the old ones. That is clear. They are done. And the injury which has been done by the issue of some of them we shall never be able to undo, particularly among some people who purchased them. But we can say this: If it is of sufficient importance, and if it is felt there is any doubt, something may be done. If the hon. member will bear in mind this single fact he will realize how difficult it is to carry into effect the regulations of a body to which all these matters would be referred: that the provinces have coequal powers with us in the creation of companies. That is our difficulty. At a conference I attended with provincial premiers it was agreed that we should have a uniform act; then when we began to discuss the terms the only uniformity was the uniformity of objections. They were very uniform indeed. To-day we cannot take that power away from them. If we set up a board and said that every company incorporated had to pass that board before it was allowed to be incorporated, the business in federal charters would be insignificant. But if we do it, as I believe we have, by imposing such restrictions upon the sale of securities as will prohibit their being sold unless under the terms of a prospectus, then I believe we have met the

difficulty. Our regulations for the issue of proapectuses are more stringent and those who issue them are asked for fuller information than is required in connection with prospectuses in any other country of the world. I say that, after some knowledge of British empire requirements, and those in the United States. I think after study it will be found that in no country of the world are there imposed as rigid and strict provisions regarding a prospectus and its contents, and the provisions for the sale of securities, as are found in our statutes. In this instance however if the minister in charge feels there is some doubt or difficulty he may refer the matter to the board, in respect of new securities.

I know the Prime Minister
has given a great deal of thought to this matter because I believe I read the first speech he made in this chamber, in 1911, when he made reference to the problem of watered stock and how it could be prevented. But that does not touch the question whether or not anything effective has really been done.
I was somewhat at a loss to follow the Prime Minister's argument. In one breath he states it .is unsound for any board to give the imprimatur of government sanction to the issue of securities; in another he states the section is to have that effect. If the Prime Minister had control of the administration of the act it would appear that there would be no references to the board, because that would be doing what is essentially unsound, namely giving the imprimatur of government sanction to security issues, thereby leading the public to think that the stock was not watered. That is just our objection. We fear that is the spirit in which the act will be administered, and that there will be no security issues referred to the tariff board at all. The tariff board, whatever can be said about the time it may have to investigate unfair trade practices, the set-up of commodity standards, and the supervision and enforcement of a great number of things, certainly will not have time to supervise the issue of securities by public companies incorporated under dominion charters. I am of the opinion that practically nothing will be done in this connection, and that we are just deluding ourselves if we think there will be. Certainly the "searchlight of publicity" being "focused on every issue of securities offered to the public" would be taken by the ordinary individual to mean something more than the filing of prospectuses. Last spring the Secretary of State said that he went as far as he could in providing for the filing of prospectuses, and last Friday he stated he was going farther, but

Trade and Industry Commission
that he was afraid further action would impinge upon provincial jurisdiction in the matter of property and civil rights, and that he had always been against the filching of provincial jurisdiction under the guise of criminal legislation, when the legislation was not in its essence criminal. So, altogether, my humble submission is that the promises of January last have not been fulfilled. I consider if we are going to have a securities control board wo should have a securities control board which would supervise all issues of securities to the public, and if we are not going to have a securities control board do not let us make a pretence of having one by passing an optional section which will impose upon the members of the tariff board, sometimes, and under some secretaries of state, a task which is beyond their ability to cope with, in view of their other extensive duties.

speechtext: Bill No. Ill, to incorporate The Community General Hospital, Alms House and Seminary of Learning of the Sisters of Charity at Ottawa, Canada.-Mr. Gagnon.

Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 101, respecting the establishment of an exchange fund.
He said: The present state of international exchanges gives cause for apprehension on the part of all persons, especially having regard to the chaotic values in the leading currencies. It was hoped in 1933 that some stabilization would be possible, and efforts, as is known, were made to that end. But alas, nothing was concluded between the great nations of the world, and the result is that there have been very great fluctuations in values-the pound sterling, the dollar abroad, and all the currencies of continental Europe.
In his remarks in making the budget statement- the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) referred to this fact; and it is in the opinion of the government desirable that machinery should be established that will at least serve some useful purpose if the occasion should arise to deal with a problem of this magnitude. Of course, it is only necessary for me to say that in Great Britain they have gone into the matter on a very tremendous scale. At one time they appropriated £150,000,000 to deal with this problem, and subsequently the amount was increased to £350,000,000 in order that the treasury might be able to take such action as might be desirable for the purpose of stabilizing the value of the pound sterling; and money for the purpose was obtained by the sale of treasury bills, that is, the sale of securities. During the last three years that fund has been operated with a very considerable measure of success. I will read from the statute, if it is desired, by which that fund was set up.
The government of the United States also provided for such a fund, resulting from the revaluation of the country's gold reserve from $20.67 to $35 an ounce. But that profit was not wholly used for that purpose; by a regulation passed in 1934 it was specifically provided that a portion of that fund might be available for that purpose, and the fund as established amounted to the very large sum of two thousand millions of dollars. It is entirely too early to express any opinion as to what the effect in that regard has been, but broadly and generally it must have served
some useful purpose. That being so, we have concluded that we can serve some useful purpose in this country at this time by revaluing our gold reserves and permitting the profit that would accrue to be held in the special fund instead of being deposited in the consolidated fund, and if the occasion arises recourse can be had to this fund to stabilize our dollar abroad.

Does
this entail an amendment to the Currency Act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, it does not. There
is no necessity for amending the Currency Act to accomplish the purpose we have in mind'. The bill, 'however, will make this permissive rather than obligatory; that is, this provision will come into force when proclamation to that effect is issued. But it is intended to proceed with the revaluation at once. That, of course, arises from the action that was taken last year in the Bank of Canada Act and the subsequent order in council passed', to which reference has already been made in the house.
The change from the S20.67 valuation to the current value of gold is, of course, largely a bookkeeping entry. It is known that the forty per cent of the gold held by the banks has by order in council been made available for their foreign balances and foreign business. The effect of the revaluation will be to enable the Bank of Canada to make the necessary bookkeeping entries and complete the transaction; but the resultant profit, as I have said, will not be dealt with as provided for in the Bank of Canada Act but retained as a fund which may be- available upon proclamation for the purpose of enabling whatever government is charged with the responsibility to utilize it for stabilization purposes.
It will be recalled that the gold purchases from the banks were on the basis of $20.67 per ounce. Some objection was made, but as a matter of fact all the gold was turned over to the Bank of Canada, and the reserves provided for under the Currency Act are twenty-five per cent in gold, under the Bank of Canada Act, with respect to our issue of paper money. This, of -course, will have the effect of extending to some extent the issue power, because twenty-five per cent on the new valuation will create more gold than under the old valuation of $20.67.
